en: Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty,
recorded by his disciple Guanding:
"If one skillfully cultivates the four samādhis so that they are harmonized and properly balanced, then by the power of the Way, [evil] will certainly not exist."
Regarding various illnesses:
even if one slightly transgresses [the precepts], the dark blades will support them,
and they shall naturally recover and be cured.
Even if various obstacles should arise like mountain peaks,
one should push death aside to preserve the remaining breaths of this life;
vowing to complete the path within the *maṇḍala*, one’s resolve must be firm.
"What sin would not be extinguished? What karma would not be transformed?
Chen Zhen and Kaishan said, and so forth.
How could the four elements and five viscera fail to be harmonized and cured?
Just as the minor spirits respectfully avoid the Hall of Śakra,
the deities of the *maṇḍala*— being great— will not falsely invade or disturb it;
furthermore, the lord of the city is firm and his guardians are powerful.
The city lord is anxious and the guards are busy;
the mind is the master of the body.
That which is called the "Heaven of Equal Birth" is a deity capable of protecting people.
If the mind is firm, it strengthens the body and spirit;
this is true even for them, let alone for the deities of the *dharmadhātu*.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains regarding the *vīrya-rākṣasa*, who adheres to the five places, and so forth.
If you simply cultivate samādhi with single-minded focus, all various ailments will dissolve.
The five methods for cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā follow the previous pattern to form ten, and so forth.
First, to distinguish what is conceivable (cintya):
Due to the causal conditions of illness, the ten dharma realms arise;
for instance, because of illness, one loses one's original resolve,
abandons meditative concentration, and slanders the Triple Gem.
Not only do they claim that past sins bring about calamity,
but they also assert that practicing virtue brings no merit, thereby giving rise to great wrong views; furthermore,
they begrudge their own bodies and seek to preserve their lives by consuming fish, meat, pungent vegetables, and alcohol at improper times and without moderation.
Or, when the illness has subsided and the body is robust, one indulges in the five desires to one's heart's content;
the wholesome mind is entirely exhausted while evil karma blazes forth,
giving rise to offenses of the superior, middling, and inferior grades.
This constitutes the creation of the three unwholesome dharma-realms due to illness.
If a person reflects that this suffering and affliction of illness is entirely brought about by their own unwholesome deeds from past lives.
Deeply feeling shame and remorse, they dare not commit wrongs;
though beset by severe illness and hardship, their virtuous mind remains unchanged as they give rise to superior,
middling, and inferior goodness.
This constitutes the creation of the three wholesome dharma-realms by means of illness.
If one encounters illness and, out of fear of birth and death, realizes that this diseased body is the retribution for prior karma; [this is the first wholesome dharma-realm].
If one constructs the cycle of birth and death and continues to transmigrate, how could it ever reach an end?
Suffering and its accumulation are precarious and fragile, following one from lifetime to lifetime, causing distress on their account.
One should therefore seek the quiescent, signless nirvana.
This is how the realm of the śrāvaka-dharma arises from illness.
Furthermore, one contemplates this illness as being my own physical and mental aggregates;
it is because of this illness that old age and death come to pass.
Death arises from birth; birth arises from past existence (*bhava*);
existence arises from grasping (*upādāna*);
and grasping arises from craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving arises from feeling;
feeling arises from contact;
contact arises from the six sense bases.
The six sense bases arise from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Form consists of the four great elements and the five faculties; name consists of the four mental aggregates.
Contemplate these faculties and elements: from what do they, in turn, arise?
The color blue arises from wood;
the color yellow arises from earth;
the color red arises from fire.
White arises from wind;
black arises from water.
Furthermore, one contemplates that wood arises from water.
Water arises from wind;
wind arises from the yang-qi of earth;
earth arises from fire.
Fire arises from wood;
wood, in turn, arises from water.
Thus they pursue one another in a cycle that begins again and again.
There is no self-arising.
Just as it is with the observation of the five external elements,
so too is it with the colors of the five internal organs.
The liver arises from the blue qi;
the heart arises from the red qi;
the lungs arise from the white qi.
The kidneys arise from black qi;
the spleen arises from yellow qi.
This liver organ is produced from its own substance.
If it arises from another,
one then knows that the liver arises from the kidneys,
and the kidneys arise from the lungs.
The lungs arise from the spleen;
the spleen arises from the heart;
the heart arises from the liver.
The liver does not arise of itself;
it arises from the kidneys.
Thus one seeks within for the four great elements and the five viscera.
Since it has no substantial body, why does it not disintegrate?
The four minds sustain it:
the consciousness-mind sustains earth, and the perception-mind sustains wind.
The mind that sustains fire and the mind that sustains water receive [these elements];
therefore, they do not perish.
Do these four minds arise spontaneously, or do they not arise spontaneously?
One then knows that the mind of volition arises from sensation;
the mind of sensation arises from perception;
and the mind of perception arises from consciousness.
Consciousness arises from past formations;
past formations arise from ignorance;
and ignorance arises from conceptual proliferation.
Delusive thoughts arise from delusive thoughts.
As the Sūtra says:
"Delusive thoughts give rise to delusive thoughts, cycling through the twelve links of dependent origination."
It is like a person suffering from a parching thirst who sees a mirage as water;
they run toward it to the south,
but though they pursue it, they do not find it, and they cry out loudly for water.
An echo in the sky calls out, "I am great! and he thinks it is himself.
He turns his head and runs north, thinking the echo is south;
thus he pursues it in all four directions but never catches it.
He was then greatly distressed;
thinking that water had entered the earth, he clawed at the ground and cried out,
his body utterly exhausted as darkness fell upon him once more.
Nor can they be obtained;
running south is like the tongue pursuing flavors,
while running north is like the ear pursuing sounds.
Running westward is a metaphor for the nose pursuing fragrance;
running eastward is a metaphor for the eye pursuing forms;
scratching the ground is a metaphor for the body pursuing tactile sensations.
Reaching the state of "darkness-as-an-allegory," the mind pursues ignorance;
thus the six sense organs roam through all sensory objects, yet not a single one can be found,
nor can the characteristic of the conjunction of causes and conditions be apprehended.
One merely exhausts oneself with suffering;
once this is realized, one no longer runs.
Because one does not run, body and mind become settled and stable.
Because the mind abides in concentration, one attains sudden awakening and realization,
giving rise to the correct wisdom of dependent origination;
one knows that this form, mind, and so forth have been quiescent in their essential nature from the very beginning.
It is neither born nor extinguished;
it is through deluded and inverted conceptualization that one speaks of birth and extinction.
If one does not follow such conceptualization, then ignorance ceases, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death.
When the old has been exhausted, one does not create the new;
just as when fire is not kindled, there is no smoke.
Since one cannot obtain ignorance, old age, death, or sickness, who then would be the one afflicted by sickness?
This is called observing the conditions that give rise to illness as the Dharma-realm of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, one observes that this illness arises entirely from cherishing one's body, life, and wealth, thereby resulting in manifold afflictions.
Furthermore, because their observance of the precepts was incomplete, they suffered from many illnesses and short lifespans;
moreover, because their mental resolve was weak, they were unable to practice patient endurance,
and thus neither their bodies nor their spirits were protected.
This is also because their power of diligence is weak and they lack the remedial protection of wholesome deeds;
it is also because they lack the power of meditative concentration.
They are shaken by illness;
this is also because their minds lack wisdom and they do not comprehend impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Having thus come to suffer this illness,
he now takes his own ailment to empathize with the ailments of others;
immediately giving rise to compassion, he brings forth vows and practices.
To practice relinquishment without lingering stinginess, to accord with principle through patient endurance,
and to apply diligent and correct intention to awaken to impermanence—
this constitutes the bodhisattva realm arising from illness as the six perfections.
Furthermore, one contemplates this illness and knows that it arises from the afflictions of deluded thoughts and inverted views from previous lives.
Such deluded thoughts possess no reality whatsoever.
Both "I" and "nirvāṇa" are empty;
this is called the realm of the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching arising from illness.
Furthermore, one contemplates that although this illness is ultimately empty, [it still manifests].
Though empty and without that which is received, one experiences various sensations.
As long as the Buddha-dharmas are not yet perfected, one should not extinguish sensation and take realization.
This is the distinct teaching for the realm of Bodhisattvas arising from illness.
Such dharmas as these arise in succession based on illness;
this is called the realm of conceptual deliberation and is not what is being contemplated here.
As for the inconceivable realm:
The mind of illness in a single thought is neither real nor existent;
it is itself the dharma-nature and the dharma-realm.
All dharmas tend toward illness, and there is no way they do not so tend.
Only the Dharma-realm is universally non-existent, devoid of the distinctions of the nine realms.
Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel is neither empty nor existent, neither prior nor posterior,
so too is illness.
Transcending words, free from marks, quiescent, and pure—
it is therefore called inconceivable.
Having realized the reality-limit of illness, what joy or sorrow could there be?
When one contemplates in this way, [the ailment] is suddenly and completely eliminated.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"Upon merely hearing these words, the illness is immediately cured."
This refers first to the contemplation of the mind and the ear.
Furthermore, there are those who are deeply afflicted and difficult to cure;
[the physician] goes to the householder’s place to compound various medicines for them.
The illness was then cured;
this is precisely the meaning of the subsequent nine contemplations.
All sentient beings possess this principle, yet they are unable to recognize it.
Seeing them sink into the sea of fragmented existence, driven by the currents of views and thoughts,
he gives rise to deep compassion,
desiring to grant them the bliss of the Path and Cessation, which is non-existent and is itself emptiness.
This is how a bodhisattva who is ill can use the contemplation of emptiness to subdue their mind.
Because the mind is subdued, the actual illness is cured;
yet, out of compassion, the provisional illness arises.
Born in the land of segmented birth,
they regard beings of that realm as if they were their only child;
when the child is ill, the parents are also ill.
He consoles them by means of his own physical illness, saying,
"If your son’s illness is cured, my parents’ illness will also be cured.
This is called consoling a sick bodhisattva through the analysis of the body.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that although this illness is empty and quiescent,
these sentient beings cannot attain liberation through emptiness alone;
one must recognize the various Dharma-gates for treating the illness of emptiness.
Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the two vehicles do not recognize this,
they flow and sink along with ignorance and lack of knowledge into the ocean of transformation; thus,
they are unable to distinguish the various grades of illnesses.
For this reason, the Buddha-dharma cannot manifest before them,
and sentient beings and their pure lands are all left unaccomplished.
For the sake of this principle, one immediately gives rise to compassion to uproot the suffering of ignorance.
Together with the joy of discerning the knowledge of the modes of the path—
this is called a sick bodhisattva being able to subdue his mind through the contemplation of the provisional.
Because the mind is subdued, the actual illness is cured.
Out of compassion, he manifests illness through skillful means and is born in the Land of Expedient Means; there,
he regards all who employ expedient means as if they were his only child.
Because the son was ill, the parents were also ill;
they comforted and exhorted their son by means of their own physical ailments.
When the son, though ignorant, recovered, the parents also recovered.
This is called the specific teaching for consoling a sick bodhisattva.
Furthermore, one contemplates that although this illness is itself the dharma-realm,
sentient beings do not yet abide in the Middle Way.
This principle has not yet been revealed; [sentient beings] follow the flow of ignorance and sink into the ocean of transformation.
As a sutra says:
"The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retributive fruition."
This is precisely the illness of cause and effect within the true retribution realm.
For this reason, one gives rise to compassion to extract beings from the suffering of ignorance and bestow upon them ultimate bliss.
This is how a bodhisattva who is ill uses the contemplation of the Middle Way to subdue his mind.
Because the mind is subdued, the actual illness is cured;
yet, out of compassion, he manifests illness through skillful means.
They are born in the Land of True Reward and regard those of the transformation body as if they were their only child.
When the child is ill, the parents are also ill.
By using his own physical illness to console and encourage his son,
the son’s ignorance is healed and the parents are likewise healed.
This is called the Perfect Teaching’s method of consoling and encouraging a sick Bodhisattva.
In this way, the three swift [qualities] arise within a single mind;
in this way, they are tamed by a single contemplation;
in this way, compassion is perfected and universal.
Thus he manifests the universal manifestation;
thus he provides consolation by preaching with a single voice.
For the sake of easy understanding, these have been analyzed as before.
To speak of it in reality, it is inconceivable compassion;
only that Vimalakīrti possesses such a dharma.
The three realities are perfectly complete, eliminating all expedient means, while the three expedients are universally manifested.
That noble person is difficult to respond to;
the king and the elder are truly gravely ill and unable to receive his final testament.
Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have eliminated the grasping at signs, their words are insufficient for practice;
as for the Bodhisattvas, they repel adventitious defilements yet often encounter setbacks.
Only Mañjuśrī’s power of the Way is his equal.
He was able because he received the imperial command by pressing the trigger.
The questioner asked: "Layman," [what do you say?]
From what cause does this illness arise?
How long has it been since it first appeared?
And how should it be extinguished?
The householder replied:
"My current illness arises from great compassion;
because sentient beings are ill, therefore I am ill."
Because the illnesses of sentient beings are healed, I am healed.
Indeed, the true illness of sentient beings arises from ignorance and craving;
as soon as ignorance and craving arise, great compassion also arises.
As soon as delusion and craving are extinguished, great compassion is also extinguished.
There are sentient beings who are healed and those who are not;
there are bodhisattvas who are ill and those who are not.
If one is free from illness, it is known that their child will recover;
if one has an illness, the transformation of the Way does not cease.
Thus, Fangzhang inquired after the illness [of the Emperor], and Maocheng suffered back pain.
All of this is the meaning: since their vows are equal to empty space, their illnesses likewise pervade the entire dharma-realm;
this is called inconceivable compassion.
The power of compassion is great;
as soon as a bodhisattva gives rise to this mind, illness is immediately cured,
without waiting for further cultivation of inferior methods.
Regarding "Dharma-joy at Tiantai" and so forth:
if one’s resolve is not sincere and one deceives sentient beings while relying on the Triple Gem,
yet harbors ulterior motives and expectations, the illness will likewise not be cured.
If one can sincerely possess great power and settle the mind,
then when practicing the human path at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) or during illness, it shall be as described above.
Realizing the essence through the arousal of the bodhicitta, with body upright and mindfulness correct,
one practices solely through śamatha and vipaśyanā,
skillfully employing the *siddhāntas* to achieve perfect harmony and appropriateness.
As soon as one sits upon it, one immediately experiences coolness;
whether this occurs suddenly or gradually,
this is called the "Great Medicine."
Furthermore, one should not be distracted by practicing other remedial methods.
Regarding "the pervasiveness of destroying [afflictions]":
when the practitioner is ill, they observe the illness.
It is caused by the disease of form or caused by the disease of mind.
If form were the disease,
then external things such as mountains and forests would all have to be diseases.
A dead person should also be considered ill;
yet corpses and mountain forests have never experienced affliction.
One should know, therefore, that form is not illness.
It is solely due to the mind’s conceptualization that one reckons this illness exists.
Now, when observing the mind of illness, it cannot be found within any of the four alternatives—it is neither self nor other.
It is neither internal nor external; it is ultimately pure.
The mind is like space; who, then, is ill?
Vimalakīrti said:
It is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element.
It does not unite with the body, because the characteristic of a body cannot be apprehended;
it does not unite with the mind, because the mind is like an illusion.
Thus, the arising of a diseased mind cannot be found.
One should not conceive of illness as non-arising,
nor as both arising and non-arising,
nor as neither arising nor non-arising.
The details regarding both the singular and the plural are all as explained above in the section on the refutation of the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas).
As for the penetration and obstruction of consciousness, one contemplates the nature of illness.
Within every sentence, one recognizes the truths, the conditions, and the means.
Contemplating the illness and contemplating wisdom, one recognizes the truths, the conditions,
and the means in every sentence, clearly and distinctly, without any doubt.
To understand characters as non-characters means to know gain and loss, as explained above.
Regarding the "harmonization of the factors of the path" (*mārga-aṅga-samādhi*):
it is like contemplating that illness is the illness of the four great elements and is impure.
If illness were separate from the four great elements, then illness would be pure; yet illness is neither the four great elements nor something apart from them.
Illness is neither pure nor impure.
It is real, yet not real; it is not non-real.
Emptiness and conventionality are neither empty nor conventional;
withering and flourishing are neither withered nor flourishing.
Such meanings as these are all non-dual and indistinguishable from the mindfulness of the body.
In this way, the sensation of illness is neither suffering nor pleasure;
the perception and mental formations of illness are neither self nor non-self;
the mind of illness is neither permanent nor impermanent.
For example, as in the aforementioned meaning,
one may achieve the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment even upon one's pillow and mat;
understanding suffering as being without suffering, one enters the pool of cool serenity.
Regarding those who assist in the path:
if one practices correct contemplation but has not yet attained resolution,
one should borrow the six types of remedies mentioned previously.
If practicing both the primary and auxiliary methods can still lead one into the Way,
how much more so when physical ailments are eliminated?
When contemplating in this way, although one may remain confined to a bed, one deeply understands the successive stages of practice.
I observe the principle of illness as it truly is,
like a lapis lazuli gem at the bottom of a deep pool.
This wisdom of my observation is merely a name.
Because the illness of the cause has not yet been eliminated, the illness of the fruit is likewise present.
If one is at a stage similar to that of understanding,
the illness of the cause is somewhat lightened and the mind of the Way matures further.
If the retributive illness is still severe, one cannot avoid various calamities;
if one enters the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
although the causal illness has been exhausted, there may still be residual retributive illness.
I should not now give rise to pride out of place by saying,
"My practice of illness is equal to that of this superior person" regarding my patient endurance.
Simply apply yourself diligently to the primary and auxiliary practices;
do not allow internal or external obstructive conditions to hinder or cause you to rest.
This is the answer to the question regarding the delay of the primary and auxiliary practices.
If one swiftly accomplishes the Way,
even in the face of illness, one can settle the mind within that illness;
remaining unmoved and non-retrogressive, the task is accomplished.
Even if you should fall ill, maintain the clarity and purity of your contemplative practice;
do not give rise to greedy attachment, and do not harbor defiled craving.
By accomplishing these ten dharmas, you will swiftly enter the stream of the Dharma.

This is called the cultivation of the Mahāyāna contemplation on the object of the realm of illness, whereby one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and obtains a great carriage.
As with the preceding cases, it may be understood accordingly, and so forth.
○ Fourth, the contemplation of the object of the characteristics of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).
The various karmas— wholesome and unwholesome— that a practitioner has performed over immeasurable eons may have already been experienced as retribution or may not yet have been experienced; however,
if the mind remains in a state of equanimity, these do not manifest.
Now, because the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā can move all karmas,
the signs of good and evil appear.
Those who doubt say:
What characteristics of the equality of the Mahāyāna could possibly be discussed?
Now, it is said that this is not so;
rather, it is precisely because the mirror of equality is pure that the images of all karmas appear.
The *Prabhāsa-megha* states that the signs of being about to realize the tenth stage all appear beforehand.
The *Āgama* states:
As he was about to realize the first fruit of the path, eighty-eight heads of snakes died before him.
There are many textual passages concerning the similarities between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one universally illumines the ten directions.
Sin and merit are merely good and evil karma.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
Since one does not waver from the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa),
your objection is invalid.
The clarification of the characteristic of activity (karma-lakṣaṇa) consists of four parts.
First, the causes and conditions for the arising of the single characteristic;
second, the characteristic of actual arising;
third, the detailed analysis.
Regarding the four types of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
their causes and conditions are both internal and external.
As for the internal,
one uses cessation and contemplation to investigate the mind;
as the mind gradually becomes clear and pure, it illuminates all that is wholesome and unwholesome.
Alternatively, one may use cessation to stop evil, for evil is precisely what one seeks to extinguish;
one may use observation to observe the good, for the good is precisely what one seeks to give rise to.
Alternatively, one may use cessation to stop evil, for evil arises from stillness.
By means of contemplation, one contemplates the good; through the contemplation of the cause of goodness, cessation is observed.
The marks of immeasurable karma emerge from within śamatha and vipaśyanā, just as myriad images naturally appear when a mirror is polished.
As for "external," the compassion of all Buddhas constantly responds to all;
yet because sentient beings lack the necessary capacity, they are unable to behold it.
By the power of śamatha and vipaśyanā, one is able to evoke all Buddhas;
the various karmas of wholesome and unwholesome dhyānas then manifest,
like holding a flower garland to show to the great assembly.
This is called internal and external causes and conditions.
If one grasps this principle,
one can minutely distinguish between transgression and merit, and between black and white, without confusion.
One who is capable of acting as a teacher of the Vaipulya sutras may subdue others;
however, for now, one should merely refine the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* so that karma may be extinguished and practice perfected.
If one seeks the Way with single-minded devotion, what need is there for convoluted discrimination of characteristics?
Second, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of karma:
since there is no sequence of before and after in their arising, we shall first explain the manifestation of the wholesome according to the convenience of the discourse.
Its characteristics are sixfold.
First, the signs of retributive fruit appear;
second, the signs of habitual causes appear;
third, the signs of retribution appear first and the signs of habituation appear later.
Fourth, the habitual karma manifests before, while the retributive karma manifests later.
Fifth, the habitual and retributive karmas manifest simultaneously.
Sixth, the timing of their manifestation—whether before or after—is indeterminate.
When various karmas manifest in the present, they differ in a myriad of ways.
To recognize these six types of mental intention without error—
how is it that one names them "causes of habituation" and "fruits of habituation"?
The Abhidharmikas say:
the cause of cultivation (*abhyāsa-hetu*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
and the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*) is the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
Furthermore, "cultivation" (vāsanā) means continuous succession.
It is the mutual production of one's own seeds;
the subsequent moment of mind arises as a continuation of the preceding one.
The preceding thought serves as the cause and the succeeding thought serves as the effect;
this principle applies to all three natures.
However, according to the masters of the treatises, it holds only for the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [states], as there is no continuity of habituation in the indeterminate.
Regarding "causes of retribution and fruits of retribution," this refers to different lifetimes.
Both the causes of cultivation and the fruits of cultivation from previous lives are termed "causes of retribution."
Because this cause draws forth its fruit, it is designated as "retribution" (vipāka);
thus, it is called the "causal condition of retribution.
The subsequent reception of a body within the five destinies is precisely the "fruit of retribution."
Upon this present body of karmic retribution, one further gives rise to the continuity of wholesome and unwholesome habits.
Considering both the causal habit and the resultant habit in relation to the previous life, this continuity is the result;
however, in relation to the future life, this continuity is the cause.
The Abhidharmikas clarify that obtaining the body of a pigeon or a sparrow is the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*),
while excessive lust is the fruit of habituation (*niṣyandaphala*).
The Śāstrakas maintain that both the pigeon’s body and the excessive lust are fruits of retribution.
Sexual misconduct arises from craving;
craving is the fruit of habitual practice.
Furthermore, the arising of afflictions in this present life constitutes the cause of habitual practice.
The completion of karma is the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
The subsequent arising of afflictions is called the fruit of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*).
Suffering and pain are called the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
If, while in meditative concentration, one perceives only various signs, this is called the manifestation of the signs of retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Because of past causes, it may also be termed a "retributive cause" (*vipākahetu*);
furthermore, these can mutually induce each other and draw forth subsequent retribution, thus receiving their respective names.
For now, it is simply judged to be the characteristic of the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*).
If, while sitting, one does not perceive various signs and a state of agitation suddenly arises in the mind,
this is the production of the causal condition for practice (*abhyāsa-hetu*), which is capable of drawing forth a future fruit.
It may also be called the "fruit of cultivation" (niṣyanda-phala) because it repays past causes;
thus, these two names are applied interchangeably.
However, for the present purpose, it is simply judged to be the "cause of cultivation" (abhyāsa-hetu).
The signs of excellence are numerous; for now, they shall be summarized according to the six perfections.
Regarding the manifestation of the sign of *dāna* (generosity):
if, while seated, one suddenly beholds a field of merit, a sublime environment, or an image of the Triple Gem.
The noble assembly of virtuous ones, parents, teachers, and monastics—
those who practice the Way—
accept one's offerings.
Sometimes they see the field of compassion receiving offerings;
sometimes they see both fields rejoicing even though they do not receive offerings;
or sometimes they see no fields at all, whether receiving or not receiving.
One may see the various articles offered for alms arranged and spread out;
or one may not see the objects of offering but only see the pure ground;
or these manifest the signs of the retribution for giving in this present life.
Either it manifests the marks of the retribution for past-life giving,
or one sees a person who habitually practices generosity approach and praise the relinquishment of gifts.
Such matters as these are all signs arising from the fruit of retribution.
Next, one perceives no such signs at all;
rather, the mind becomes filled with a profound sense of earnestness, desiring to practice giving and to offer respectful worship to the Triple Gem, one’s parents, and the teachers and monks.
Whether it be out of compassion for the suffering of poverty and a desire to provide relief,
or through mastery of the dharma-gate of giving (dāna) such that one understands it thoroughly and with personal clarity—
such states of mind as these are all signs of the arousal of the causal conditions for cultivation.
Either this mind arises first and one subsequently perceives the signs of retribution,
or one first perceives the signs of retribution and subsequently gives rise to this mind;

Question:
After Māra has finished disturbing [the practitioner], wholesome dharmas subsequently arise.
Is this because it is the nature of things (dharmatā) that winter passes and spring arrives?
Answer:
It is not necessarily so;
there are indeed difficult objections that prevent even excellent dharmas from arising.
Māra is brought about by evil conditions;
goodness is produced by the power of the mind.
As the *Śāstra* states:
In the past, Śākyamuni lived in an evil age when there was no Buddha in the world;
though he sought the Dharma with diligent perseverance, he could not obtain it.
The Māra transformed himself into a brahmin and spoke deceitfully:
"There is a single verse of a Buddha;
if you can use your skin as paper, your bones as a pen, and your blood as ink, I shall give it to you."
The Bodhisattva delighted in the Dharma;
he then flayed his own skin, dried it in the sun, and prepared it for writing verses.
Thereupon, Māra vanished.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, caused them to surge forth from below and preached the profound sutras for them,
whereby they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This may be taken as proof, and so forth.
